*This version cleans up the run-on sentence structure, enhances the rhythm, and elevates the vocabulary while preserving the raw humanity of the scene.*

> "I attempted to smoke one or two, but they were hopelessly stale—snapping like dry twigs or crumbling beneath my fingers as I tried to roll them. Lighting a match proved futile, and returning them to the refrigerator was no longer an option; it was far too late for that. Even dampening the wrappers filled my mouth with pulverized outer leaf—a yield of Lancaster or eastern Virginia, as my deep-seated heritage and knowledge of cigars assured me. 
> 
> In a moment of sheer, frantic frustration, I cast handfuls of them out of my third-floor window. To my horror, four or five street people were sitting on my stoop, scrambling to catch them as if they had suddenly struck wealth. I felt an immediate wave of remorse; no one should be degraded in such a manner. Driven by reckless impulse, I ran downstairs to explain, but they were already smoking. Having nothing else to offer—as we ourselves were subsisting on beans—I simply sat down and joined them. Every so often, we looked up at the open window above, and one of us spat into an empty can. We were visionaries."

---

### Option 2: Smooth & Expressive
*This version stays closer to the conversational flow of the original while polishing the phrasing and punctuation.*

> "I tried one or two, but they were stale—snapping like dry sticks and crumbling as I rolled them. A lit match was useless, and it was far too late to put them back in the refrigerator. Upon testing a couple of the cigars, I found them thoroughly dried out. Handling them caused them to snap like brittle twigs or disintegrate into dust, rendering any attempt to light them futile. Attempting to restore their moisture in the refrigerator was no longer a viable remedy. Even moistening the wrappers left fragments of outer leaf in my mouth—tobacco I instinctively identified as originating from Lancaster or eastern Virginia, thanks to an inherent expertise passed down through my lineage. 

Overcome by a sudden, erratic impulse, I grabbed clusters of them and hurled them out of my third-floor window. To my dismay, four or five unhoused people sitting on my front stoop scrambled after the falling cigars as though they had stumbled upon a treasure. I feel deeply remorseful for subjecting anyone to such a humiliating spectacle; my actions were frantic and unreasoned. 

I rushed downstairs to clarify the situation, but they were already puffing away. Because my own household was barely getting by on a basic diet of beans, I had no actual food or money to share with them. Consequently, I took a seat on the steps and joined in the smoke session. Every so often, our eyes drifted upward toward the unclosed window above, and someone discharged spit into a tin container. 

We were dreamers who possessed a grander foresight.
outputs.L3:
It began with a careless gesture born of frustration. Cleaning out the cluttered drawers of my third-floor apartment, I came across a handful of old cigars. Forgotten for months, they were brittle, unravelling, and entirely ruined. Without a second thought, I pushed open the drafty window and tossed the stale tobacco out into the gray afternoon air, watching them fall toward the pavement below.

Leaning out to close the sash, a sudden movement on the street caught my eye. A small group of men, huddled against the chill in threadbare coats, had seen the falling cigars. Instantly, they scrambled across the concrete, stooping and diving to gather the broken stems from the dirt. The sight struck me like a blow to the chest. What had been a mindless act of discarding rubbish had transformed into an accidental cruelty. Looking down from my high window, I felt an intense wave of guilt; I had inadvertently played the part of a callous aristocrat throwing scraps to the desperate, degrading them in the process.

Driven by a desperate need to undo the humiliation, I turned and rushed down the three flights of stairs. But as my hand touched the heavy front door, reality checked me. I reached into my pockets, searching for something—anything—I could offer by way of a proper gesture. My fingers met only lint and a loose key. I was as broke as the men outside, my own kitchen holding nothing more than half a loaf of stale bread and a box of cheap tea. I had no food to share, no money to give, and no grand gesture to offer. All I had was my own embarrassment.

I stepped out onto the cold stone stoop. The men were dusting off the dry, crumbled leaves, trying to salvage what they could. 

"I'm sorry," I said, my voice cutting through the quiet street. "I didn't mean to throw them out like that. They’re stale—they’re completely ruined. I should have just binned them."

The men looked up, surprised not by the poor quality of the tobacco, but by the apology itself. One of them, an older man with deep lines etched around his eyes, shrugged with a faint, weary smile. "A smoke’s a smoke, mate," he said softly, striking a match against the heel of his boot.

I didn't walk back inside. Instead, I sat down beside him on the cold steps. Taking one of the cracked, low-quality cigars from the pile, I struck my own match and lit it. One by one, the rest of the group joined us, sitting shoulder-to-shoulder on the stoop. 

We smoked together in silence. The tobacco was harsh, biting the back of the throat and tasting of dust and age, but nobody complained. As the gray plumes of smoke drifted up into the bleak sky, the initial awkwardness melted away, replaced by a quiet, unspoken solidarity. 

In that shared space of quiet endurance, something shifted inside me. Though we were all bound by the weight of financial hardship, the feeling of humiliation vanished. Sitting there among them, wrapped in a haze of bitter smoke, I felt an almost transcendent sense of connection. These were not men to be pitied; they possessed a quiet, resilient dignity. Looking through the thin veil of smoke at their weathered faces, I saw them not as the impoverished, but as visionaries—men who understood the true, stripped-down essence of survival, finding warmth and community in the very scraps the world had thrown away.

The cedar box had sat forgotten in the corner of my study for far too long, a casualty of neglect in a room filled with dust and half-finished drafts. When I finally pulled one of the dark, handsome cylinders from its bed, the wrapper cracked softly beneath the pressure of my thumb. I tried to clip the end, but the leaf pulverized into brittle chaff. I struck a match anyway, drawing in a breath, hoping to find the rich, earthy warmth I remembered. Instead, my mouth filled with the acrid taste of scorched dust and dry air. The cigar was utterly dead, its essential oils dried to nothing.

In a fit of petty, evening irritation—frustrated by the small disappointment after a long day—I grabbed the entire box, marched to the window, and heaved the sash upward. The cold night air rushed in, smelling of rain and distant coal smoke. Without a second thought, I overturned the box, dumping two dozen stale, fragile cigars out into the dark space of the alley below. They tumbled through the three stories of air like withered autumn leaves.

I turned to walk away, but a sudden sound pulled me back to the ledge. 

It was the dark, hurried scraping of leather on wet cobblestones. Leaning out into the chill, I looked down. From the alcoves and shadowed doorways across the street, three figures had materialized. They were threadbare, stooped men, wrapped in coat fragments and tied up in twine against the dampness. They were on their knees in the dim glow of the streetlamp, frantically sweeping their hands across the gutter, gathering the fallen cigars. Even as the delicate tubes crumbled in their rough, calloused hands, they scooped up the fragments, stuffing the loose tobacco into their pockets with wild, desperate efficiency.

A sharp, sick knot tightened in my stomach. From my warm, elevated sanctuary on the third floor, I had meant only to discard rubbish. But to the men below, my casual gesture of waste had looked like an act of cruel patronage—a wealthy man throwing scraps into the dirt for the dogs to fight over. I had forced human beings to scramble in the gutter for my trash, simply because I had been too lazy to throw it in the scuttle. The height of my apartment suddenly felt nauseating, a physical representation of an unearned, unfeeling distance.

Instinct took over before my pride could intervene. I grabbed my heavy wool coat from the rack and a box of long wooden matches from the mantelpiece. I didn't take the lift; I ran down the three flights of stairs, the cold iron handrail chilling my palm, until I burst through the heavy front doors and stepped onto the street level.

The men froze as the heavy doors slammed shut behind me. One of them, an older man with a face carved deep by frost and hunger, instinctively flinched back, clutching a handful of broken tobacco leaves to his chest, expecting a scolding, or worse, the police.

"Wait," I said, my voice quiet in the still night air. "Please."

I walked slowly toward the stoop, taking care not to make any sudden movements. The cold of the stone pavement seeped immediately through the soles of my slippers. I reached into my pocket, pulled out the box of matches, and sat down on the bottom step of the stoop, right beside them.

The old man looked at me, his eyes wide and wary beneath a battered cap. 

Without saying a word, I reached out and gently touched the cuff of his coat, pointing to the crushed half of a cigar he held in his fist. He hesitated, then slowly raised it to his lips. I struck a match against the side of the box. The small yellow flame bloomed between us, casting a warm, flickering light across our faces, bridging the space between the third floor and the pavement.

I held the flame steady for him. He leaned in, taking a long, ragged pull until the end of the broken tobacco lit up in a bright, cherry-red glow. Smoke curled between us into the night air, smelling no longer of bitter decay, but of something shared and human.

The other two men slowly stepped out of the shadows and drew closer. I didn't stand up. I remained there on the cold stone, striking match after match, lighting their salvaged scraps until all four of us sat shoulder-to-shoulder on the stoop, burning away the dark and the cold, one draft of smoke at a time.

Nestled on the eastern edge of Virginia’s historic Northern Neck, **Lancaster County, Virginia**, is a region where serene waterways, rich American history, and small-town coastal charm seamlessly converge. Bordered by the Rappahannock River and the Chesapeake Bay, Lancaster offers a tranquil escape into a world defined by maritime traditions and timeless Southern hospitality.

### A Tapestry of American History

Lancaster County holds a deeply significant place in the narrative of early America. Established in 1651, the county is steeped in colonial heritage. It is famously the birthplace of Mary Ball Washington, the mother of the nation’s first president, George Washington. Visitors can explore this legacy at the Mary Ball Washington Museum and Library, located in the historic courthouse village of Lancaster.

Another crown jewel of the area’s history is Historic Christ Church. Built in 1735, this National Historic Landmark is considered one of the finest and best-preserved examples of colonial Georgian architecture in the United States. Walking through its grounds offers a rare, unaltered glimpse into 18th-century Virginia life.

### Distinctive Towns and Communities

While the county seat, Lancaster, serves as the historical anchor, the surrounding towns each bring their own unique flavor to the area:

*   **Kilmarnock:** Serving as the vibrant commercial hub of the county, Kilmarnock features walkable streets lined with charming boutiques, antique shops, art galleries, and local eateries. It offers a lively small-town atmosphere complete with community parks and year-round events.
*   **Irvington:** Known for its quiet elegance, Irvington is a picturesque resort town situated along Carters Creek. It is home to the renowned Tides Inn, a world-class resort that has drawn visitors for decades, as well as boutique wineries, championship golf courses, and upscale dining.
*   **White Stone:** Located near the foot of the impressive Robert O. Norris Jr. Memorial Bridge, White Stone is the gateway to Lancaster County. It remains deeply tied to the local waterborne economy and serves as a bustling center for fresh seafood and marine services.

### Life on the Water and Outdoors

For nature lovers and outdoor enthusiasts, Lancaster, Virginia, is a paradise. With hundreds of miles of shoreline, life here naturally revolves around the water. Sailing, powerboating, kayaking, and paddleboarding are everyday pastimes. The region is also a crucial stop on the Virginia Oyster Trail, where visitors can sample legendary Chesapeake Bay oysters fresh from local waters.

On land, **Belle Isle State Park** offers over 700 acres of tidal wetlands, farmland, and forests along the Rappahannock River. The park provides opportunities for camping, hiking, biking, birdwatching, and guided canoe trips, allowing visitors to immerse themselves in the pristine coastal ecosystem.

### A Hidden Gem of the Chesapeake

Whether you are looking to explore early American history, indulge in fresh farm-to-table and sea-to-table cuisine, or simply unwind by the water as the sun sets over the bay, Lancaster, Virginia, delivers a unique and memorable experience. It remains one of the mid-Atlantic's most captivating hidden gems—a place where the past is cherished, the pace is relaxed, and the beauty of the Chesapeake Bay is always within view.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, beat-style literary vignette about someone living in poverty who throws a batch of ruined cigars out their apartment window, ending with the sentence: "We were visionaries."
counterfactuals.output:
The radiator rattled its dry iron bone-song into the four-dollar gloom of the third-floor walk-up, where the wallpaper hung like shed snake skin and the rain beat a frantic bop against the soot-stained glass. We sat on the sag-backed mattress, soaked to the ankles, staring down at the disaster: a score of hand-rolled cigars, salvaged from a basement shop with our last silver dime, now ruined—drenched by the roof leak into soggy, split, unsmokeable brown sponges spilling wet guts across the linoleum. 

Leo didn't weep; he just laughed that wild, jagged midnight laugh that rattled the chipped teacups. He heaved the window sash up into the freezing dark, letting the diesel-scented gale wash over our faces, and scooped up the fat, wet duds by the handful. He pitched them out into the neon abyss—dark brown meteors arcing through the streetlamp glare, plunging three stories down to splash uselessly in the oil-slicked gutter of 6th Street. We leaned out over the cold iron sill and watched them go, throwing away our last earthly luxury, laughing at the rain and the cops and the hunger, burning up the night with no fire at all. 

We were visionaries.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a first-person narrative about an accidental moment of solidarity with homeless people on a stoop. Make it sound raw and gritty, like Charles Bukowski or Raymond Carver.
counterfactuals.output:
The rain had that sour, metallic smell it gets when it rolls off rusty fire escapes and hits the hot asphalt. My feet were soaked. I was wearing twenty-dollar shoes from a discount bin, and the right sole had split like an overcooked hot dog about four blocks back. 

I didn't care much about the shoes. I cared about the neon sign in my head that was screaming for a bed, or a drink, or just five minutes where gravity didn't feel like a fat man standing on my chest.

I turned the corner off 4th Street and my knees just quit. I dropped onto the concrete stoop of an old brownstone with board-up windows. It was dry under the rusted awning, barely. 

That’s when a shadow in the corner moved and cleared its throat. Sounded like a wet rag getting dragged across coarse sandpaper.

"You're on my leg, pal."

I flinched, pulled back. My eyes adjusted to the yellow gloom of the streetlamp. There were three of them squeezed into the alcove, wrapped in layers of damp wool and dark plastic garbage bags. The speaker was an older guy with a beard that looked like it had been chewed on by goats. His eyes were small, red-rimmed, and sharp.

"Sorry," I said. My voice sounded thin, like cheap paper. "I didn't see you."

"Yeah," the middle one said. He was younger, maybe thirty, but his teeth were mostly gone and he had a dark bruise flower blooming over his cheekbone. "Nobody sees shit when they’re walking."

I meant to get up. I really did. I was wearing a cheap tie and a wrinkle-stained dress shirt from a day job that paid me just enough to starve slowly. I was supposed to be better off than them. That’s what the pamphlet said. But I couldn't move my legs. 

I pulled out a pack of smokes. Half-crushed. Two left. 

"Got a light?" the goat-beard guy asked.

I dug in my pocket. Pulled out a plastic disposable lighter. The thumb wheel was stuck. I scraped it twice, three times. Nothing. Just sparks. My hand was shaking. I was tired, man. Just bone-deep, rotten tired. The kind of tired where you start thinking about sleeping under a moving train.

Goat-beard reached out a hand. The skin was dark with ground-in street dirt, the nails thick and yellow. He didn't snatch it. He just took the lighter, held it inside his coat, blew on it, and flicked it once. A clean yellow flame. 

He lit my cigarette first. 

I took a pull. The cheap tobacco burned my throat, and for a second, the universe felt like it was holding its breath. Then he lit his own stub—a mashed-up filter he’d probably pulled out of a gutter. 

"Rough one?" he asked. 

"Lost my apartment," I said. It came out before I could stop it. I hadn't told anyone yet. Not my boss, not the landlord who put the paper on the door, nobody. "Deposit’s gone. Car broke down in August."

The guy with the bruised cheekbone made a quiet clicking sound with his tongue. Not pity. Just recognition. Like I’d just told him the weather was wet.

Goat-beard reached into the folds of a heavy military coat and pulled out a pint bottle of Popov vodka. There was about two inches of clear liquid sloshing around the bottom. He uncrewed the red plastic cap, took a quick, practiced swig that didn't even make his eyes water, and handed it to me.

"Drink," he said. "It don't fix the shoes, but it stops the leak in your chest."

I looked at the mouth of the bottle. A week ago, I would’ve thought about germs. Hepatitis. Whatever else they warn you about in the clean, well-lit places. But the rain was coming down harder now, hammering the pavement like gravel thrown against glass, and the cold was crawling up my spine like a centipede.

I took the bottle and drank. It tasted like rubbing alcohol and rusty pipes. It hit my stomach and exploded like a small flare. 

I passed it back. "Thanks."

"Name's Artie," goat-beard said. "That's Miller. The quiet one sleeping on the mailboxes is Frenchy."

"Henry," I said.

Just then, a black-and-white cruiser turned the corner, rolling slow. The spotlight on the driver's side flicked on, sweeping the wet sidewalks like a searchlight over a prison yard. It hit the stoop. The bright white beam pinned the four of us there—the three ghosts in garbage bags and the idiot in the ruined suit. 

Instinctively, I leaned back, shrinking into the dark corner with them. Artie didn't move an inch. He just stared right down the beam of light, his jaw set, his eyes dead. Miller pulled his hood down a little lower.

The cruiser paused. The engine idled, a heavy, mechanical heartbeat in the rain. We sat there together, shoulder to shoulder, smelling of wet dog, sour alcohol, and stale tobacco. For ten seconds, we were the exact same piece of garbage to the guy behind that wheel. 

The light flicked off. The cruiser rolled away, its red taillights reflecting in the puddles like two drops of fresh blood.

Miller spit into the gutter. "Pigs."

"Yeah," Artie said softly. 

He didn't offer the bottle again. He just put the cap back on and shoved it deep into his pocket. We sat there in silence for another twenty minutes while the storm blew itself out. Nobody talked about the rent, or the police, or the cold. We just watched the water run down the curb, dragging cigarette butts and candy wrappers into the storm drain.

Around three in the morning, the rain stopped. 

I pushed myself up off the step. My knees popped. My right foot squelched in the ruined shoe.

"I gotta try and walk it off," I said.

Artie looked up. He tossed my cheap lighter back to me. I caught it.

"Watch the grate on 5th," he said, turning back toward his coat. "It’s slick."

"Right," I said. 

I started walking down the street. The air was cold enough to show my breath, but the burning in my stomach hadn't entirely gone out. I didn't feel good, and I didn't feel saved. But as I turned the corner into the dark, I knew I wasn't walking alone anymore, even if I was by myself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a story about throwing away old cigars from a third-story window, feeling guilty when street people grab them, and ultimately going downstairs to sit and smoke with them.
counterfactuals.output:
The humidor had sat on top of Arthur’s bookshelf for five years, a heavy mahogany relic from a promotion he’d long since ceased to care about. Inside were two dozen Romeo y Julietas—once rich, oily, and expensive, now dry as autumn leaves. 

It was a Tuesday night, cold and sharp, and Arthur was in the middle of a ruthless, solitary cleaning frenzy. He opened the humidor, pinched one of the cigars, and heard the wrapper crack beneath his fingers. Useless. He walked over to the bay window of his third-floor apartment, unlatched the heavy glass, and leaned out into the bite of the evening air.

Instead of walking the three flights down to the dumpster, he yielded to a moment of lazy impulse. He grabbed a handful of the brown cylinders and tossed them into the night. 

They tumbled through the glow of the streetlight, spinning like little batons before hitting the damp asphalt of the alley below. He grabbed the rest, letting them rain down in a second, careless volley. 

Arthur was about to pull the window shut when he saw the movement in the shadows across the street.

From beneath the awning of the closed dry cleaner, two men pushed themselves up from a mattress of flattened cardboard. A third man, leaning against a warm laundry vent, stepped out into the light. Arthur watched, frozen, as they hurried toward the scattered cigars.

They weren't angry. They were eager. One man went to his knees, his fingerless gloves sweeping the wet pavement to retrieve three intact cigars. Another picked one up, brought it to his nose, and let out a soft, crackling laugh that floated all the way up to Arthur’s window.

A knot of hot, sick guilt tightened instantly in Arthur’s stomach. 

From his third-story perch—warm, well-lit, elevated—he had tossed away his garbage, and below him, human beings were scrambling for it like birds fighting over breadcrumbs. He hadn't meant to mock them, but the geography of the moment made the cruelty absolute. He was the lord in the tower; they were the desperate below.

He pulled back from the window, the cold air suddenly feeling like an accusation. He looked at the empty mahogany box on his table, then down at his hands.

Arthur picked up his heavy winter coat. From the top drawer of his desk, he pulled out his old brass Zippo lighter and a double-bladed cigar cutter he hadn’t used in half a decade. He checked his coat pocket and found three last cigars he had missed—stored in individual, sealed glass tubes, completely preserved from the air.

He didn't wait for the elevator. He took the stairs three at a time, his boots clattering against the concrete, the guilt driving him downward until he pushed through the heavy front door and stepped onto the street.

The air smelled of wet asphalt and diesel exhaust. Across the alley, the three men were huddled under the streetlight. One of them was fruitlessly striking a dead plastic lighter against a cigar with a cracked foot.

Arthur swallowed hard, feeling small, and walked over.

"Hey," Arthur said, keeping his voice quiet so as not to startle them.

The men turned. The tallest of them, wearing a faded navy jacket wrapped in duct tape, narrowed his eyes. "We aren't doing anything wrong, man. Just picking up what was dropped."

"I know," Arthur said. He stopped a few feet away, pulling his hands from his pockets so they could see them. "I dropped them. From up there." He pointed up to the illuminated third-story window.

The men looked up, then back at Arthur. A tense silence stretched between them.

"I shouldn't have thrown them," Arthur said, the honesty stark in the cold air. "It was lazy, and it was disrespectful. I'm sorry."

The man with the dead lighter looked at Arthur for a long moment, then down at the crushed cigar in his hand. "They're pretty dry, boss. But tobacco is tobacco."

"The ones on the ground are ruined," Arthur said. He reached into his coat and pulled out the three glass tubes. "These aren't. They're still good."

He handed one to each of the men. They took them carefully, holding the glass up to the streetlight like it was liquid gold. 

Arthur then reached into his pocket and pulled out the cutter and the brass Zippo. He stepped closer. "Here. Let me show you—you gotta snip the cap first, or it won't draw right."

He clipped the end of the tall man's cigar, then flicked the Zippo. The yellow flame flared, smelling faintly of lighter fluid. The tall man leaned in, puffing gently until the foot of the cigar glowed a deep, cherry red. A thick, sweet plume of smoke drifted into the night air.

"Damn," the man murmured, taking a slow step back and looking at the burning tip. "That's smooth. I'm Marcus, by the way."

"Arthur."

Arthur cut and lit the cigars for the other two men—Dave and a quiet older man who just called himself 'Sarge.' 

When they were all lit, Arthur looked at his own hands. He didn't have a fourth cigar, but Marcus looked at the glass tube in his hand, then at Arthur. 

"You got a light, but you aren't smoking, Arthur?" Marcus asked, a faint smile touching his mouth. 

Dave, who had picked up one of the drier, unbroken cigars from the sidewalk earlier, clipped it with Arthur's cutter and handed it to Arthur. "It ain't in a glass tube, but it’ll light."

Arthur took it. He lit it with his Zippo, drawing the bitter, dry smoke into his mouth. It tasted of earth, wood, and age, a little harsh on his throat, but he didn't care.

Arthur walked over to the curb and sat down. His expensive trousers pressed against the cold, grimy concrete. After a second, Marcus sat down next to him, pulling his jacket tighter. Dave and Sarge leaned against the brick wall beside them.

Above them, the third-story window remained open, a square of yellow light high up in the dark. But down on the street, four men sat together in the cold, watching the blue smoke rise into the night, sharing a flame.

counterfactuals.output:
The concrete stoop of 4th Street still held the suffocating heat of a July afternoon, radiating through the thin denim of Marcus’s jeans. In his shirt pocket rested a crumpled paper bag containing two "White Owl" cigars—dry, unravelling, and completely stale. He had spent his last four dollars on them, a stupid, selfish impulse when the landlord’s warning notice was already taped to his door. The guilt sat heavy in his throat, thicker than the exhaust fumes drifting from the avenue.

"You're burning paper, man," a voice rasped from the doorway. 

Sal stepped out, his knees popping as he sat down two steps above Marcus. Between his calloused hands, Sal held a dented, handleless saucepan. A cloud of steam rose into the twilight, carrying the earthy, salty scent of smashed pinto beans, spiced with a stray packet of Goya seasoning.

"They were cheap," Marcus muttered, staring down at the fraying tobacco leaf cracking beneath his thumb. "Bought 'em instead of milk. Dumb."

Sal didn't offer a sermon. Poverty in the city didn't leave much room for judgment; everyone took turns drowning. Instead, Sal reached into his jacket pocket, pulled out two scratched plastic spoons stolen from a fast-food joint, and handed one down to Marcus.

"Eat," Sal said simply, setting the hot pot on the step between them. "I cooked 'em down with water and an onion stub. Ain't fancy, but it fills the noise."

Marcus hesitated, the weight of his foolishness tying his stomach in knots. But the aroma was an eviction notice to his pride. He scraped a spoon against the bottom of the aluminum pot and blew on the hot, brown mush. It was warm, heavy, and tasted overwhelmingly like comfort. They ate in silence, the rhythm of their clinking spoons matching the distant rumble of the subway beneath the street grate.

When the pot was scraped clean, Marcus reached into his pocket and pulled out the second dry cigar. He handed it up to Sal. 

Sal took it, feeling the stale, brittle wrap with practiced fingers. He didn't complain. He just struck a match against the concrete, the small orange flame illuminating the deep, weathered lines of his face. He lit Marcus’s first, then his own.

They sat together on the crumbling stoop as the city melted into midnight. The cigars tasted like burnt hay and dust, but as the acrid smoke rose to mingle with the city air, Marcus felt the sharp edge of his shame soften. They had no money, no safety net, and no promises for tomorrow. But right now, on a hard stone step, they had smoke, they had beans, and they were not alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a nostalgic yet dark paragraph from the perspective of an expert on tobacco who is down on his luck, making a foolish mistake with his last stash of cigars.
counterfactuals.output: I used to roll a vintage 1992 Sir Winston between my fingers, listening for that subtle, oily yield that signaled a masterwork of Cuban soil and decades of patient fermentation—a rich, lost symphony of cocoa, cedar, and aged leather. Tonight, shivering in a cold, water-stained room that smelled of mildew and cheap gin, those glory days felt like a fever dream, leaving me with nothing to my name but a single, forgotten box of Cohiba Espléndidos, bone-dry and brittle from years of my own neglect. Desperate for a taste of the man I used to be and stupid with cold, I committed a cardinal sin that would have made my younger self weep: in a frantic attempt to rapidly rehydrate the parched leaves, I held the exposed cigars directly over the scalding steam of a boiling tea kettle. I watched in horrified, slow-motion clarity as the violent heat tore through the delicate Maduro wrappers, bursting their pristine veins and swelling the inner binder until the precious rolls split wide open, weeping bitter, hot moisture. As the cigars melted into a soggy, ruined pulp, the drafty room filled not with the creamy perfume of my vanished life, but with the sickening stench of wet rot, leaving me clutching warm trash in the dark, bankrupt of even my memories.
